# Decisions `[DRAFT]`

> A dated log of architectural and tactical decisions that shape GL's current form. Each entry answers: **what was the choice, when, and why**. Entries are append-only. When a previous decision is revised, do not delete it — add a new entry that supersedes it, and annotate the old one.

Entries sorted reverse-chronological (newest first). Unknown precise dates are flagged.

<a id="d-340"></a>
## D-340 — one build flag, `GL_CUDA`, gates the CUDA route on every host; the Makefile builds it with `USE_CUDA=1` (2026-09-04,, maintainer-approved item 8)


**The choice.** The CUDA route was gated by `_WIN32`, so Linux could never run it and — since the GPU full-run squash — the Linux processor build did not even link (`gpu/phase2_sealing.cpp` references the `.cu` unit's download methods). Now `GL_CUDA` is the single gate: the Visual Studio project defines it; the Makefile defines it under `USE_CUDA=1`, compiles `src/gpu/*.cu` and `src/tests/*.cu` with nvcc for `sm_89` and `sm_120`, and links `cudart` (`CUDA_HOME`, `NVCC`, `CUDA_ARCH` overridable); the sealing unit and the CUDA tests compile only under the flag; a build without it asserts at prover construction when a CUDA route is selected. Default `USE_CUDA=0` keeps the macOS CI runner and any toolkit-free Linux host building the processor binary.

**Why.** The maintainer's release-13 item 8: Ubuntu must be able to use the GPU, and the processor binary must build without a CUDA toolkit. One flag, defined by the build system, keeps the routes byte-identical by contract on both hosts and makes the missing-toolkit case a build-time choice instead of a silent platform difference.

**Gate.** Windows full rebuild + 1626/1626; WSL `make USE_CUDA=1` (2 min 7 s) + 1626/1626 and `make` (processor) + 1626/1626; the item-7 run matrix in `docs/release13/release13_ledger.md`.

<a id="d-339"></a>
## D-339 — the Lean export runs inside every pipeline run, from a selection derived from the run, into the mode's own proof-graph folder (2026-09-04,, maintainer directive)


**The choice (maintainer, release 13).** `proof_export/live.py` derives the selection from the run — the anchor blocks of `global_theorem_list.txt`, the computed theorem-list hash, coverage recorded instead of pinned, same-list imports and external citations resolved by content (alpha match, else the validator's structural search with inferred head aliases) — and writes certificates, a complete Lake project and the kernel-check log into `files/full_proof_graph/lean_export/` (Peano + Gauss, full run) and `files/shortcut/full_proof_graph/lean_export/` (FTA, depending on the full-run export copied in). The incubator graph gets no export (unsound-by-design back reformulation). Toolchain absent → one notice, no export, no crash; present → export and kernel check, a kernel failure fails the run. The tracked release package stays; the live builder is its re-pin tool.

**Why.** A customer must see the Lean check as part of the product, not as a maintainer command; the tracked, index-pinned selections could not follow a fresh proof graph (every prover generation moved theorem indices), and manual re-pinning was the recurring release chore. The output sits next to the HTML so the website copy carries it and every proof page can link its Lean twin.

**Rejected.** Regenerating the tracked `lean_export/` on every run (dirty tracked artifacts on every sandbox run; the release script owns that package). Hard-requiring Lean (a customer PC without Lean must still run).

**The FTA export is independent of the main path (maintainer ruling, 2026-09-04).** The shortcut's only theorem input is its tracked externals snapshot, which need not match the latest main run, and its Lean export depends on nothing else: the snapshot's base-form rows become two certificate-shaped theorem lists (Peano-anchored, Gauss-anchored), every cited external is resolved by content against them, and each enters Lean as a proposition parameter of the citing theorem in a self-contained Lean project (own definitions module, `lake build` as the check). The full run's export is never read by the shortcut.

**Base-form adaptation.** The FTA batch compiles its own compacts, so a compact citation must meet the externals' base-form spelling — beyond the alias-plus-premise-permutation check of D-294. The builder adds a third resolution stage: both spellings are brought to a registry-independent base form (exactly the spontaneous compacts unfolded, as the prover's `expandToBaseForm`; config-defined operators kept as atoms; commutative connectives in shape order; double negation cancelled) and compared alpha-equivalently under a premise permutation; the declared adaptation carries `base_form: true`. The checked equivalence stays a Python-side structural validation of the target proposition FTA receives as a parameter; the Lean interface is unchanged.

**Gate.** `tests/test_proof_export_live.py`, `tests/test_lean_existence_compacts.py`; a live main-graph export with `lake build` green; a shortcut export with the FTA compile green; release-13 ledger.

**The tracked package is retired (maintainer decision, 2026-09-04).** The index-pinned selections (`peano_full_64`, `gauss_main_29`, `fta_shortlist_79`, and their historical siblings), the generated certificates under `proof_export/generated/`, and the generated modules and manifests under `lean_export/` are no longer tracked. The release ships the two run exports as they are: `release_public.py::check_live_lean_exports` requires both with a green `kernel_check.log`, re-runs `lake build` in each, runs the renderer contract tests, and the copy is byte-checked; the private snapshot overlays the same two folders. The tracked `lean_export/` keeps only the Lake skeleton the live export copies. Two historical certificates survive as renderer-test fixtures under `tests/fixtures/lean_certificates/`; the FTA contract tests read the live shortcut export and skip when none is on disk.

<a id="d-338"></a>
## D-338 — the processor route is the product default of every run; `main.py --GPU` selects CUDA for the whole run (2026-09-04,, maintainer directive)


**The choice (maintainer directive, release 13 preparation).** `ProverParameters::use_gpu` defaults false, no shipped config pins a batch to CUDA (the explicit `use_gpu: true` of `ConfigIncubatorPeano1.json` is gone), and `main.py` gains `--GPU`, which is exactly `--phase2-backend cuda` applied to every batch of the run — full or shortcut. The shortcut's own default moves from CUDA to the processor route. `--phase2-backend cpu|cuda` stays as the explicit oracle override; naming both `--GPU` and `--phase2-backend` asserts. A selected CUDA route that finds device, driver or runtime missing asserts, as before ([I-211](30_invariants.md#i-211)). Agents pass `--GPU` on every run (the project conventions).

**Why.** User experience on a customer PC: GL must run without a GPU and without any CUDA installation, so the bare `python main.py` has to be the processor run. The CUDA route stays the agents' route because it is several times faster and byte-identical by contract, so the development host loses nothing but one flag.

**What ships.** Nothing new: the executable links the static CUDA runtime, which loads `nvcuda.dll` and `nvcudart_hybrid64.dll` from the NVIDIA driver at `--GPU` time only; the processor route touches neither, and the import table names no CUDA library.

**Supersedes** the default clause of [D-329](#d-329) (CUDA as the batch default) and the shortcut CUDA default of 2026-09-01; batch ownership of the route and the CUDA/SSD exclusion are unchanged.

**Gate.** `test_phase2_projection.cpp` (`backend_defaults_to_processor_and_accepts_explicit_cuda`); shortcut and full runs on both routes byte-identical (release-13 ledger, item 7).

<a id="d-336"></a>
## D-336 — the remaining-args edge key is built in a caller-owned stack buffer, never at an arena cursor mark: the G-72 root cause and its fix (2026-09-03)


**The root cause (found by the permanent G-72 key-family dump on the first firing after the trap campaign).** The failing edge key the removal looked up read `[-842150451 × 10, 4, 42]` — `0xCDCDCDCD`, the arena poison byte. `remArgsEdgeKeyInto` allocated the key on the slot's gen-scratch arena and returned only its length; all four callers then read the key back at `gArena.resolve(mark)` with `mark` captured BEFORE the allocation. `LbArena::alloc` aligns the cursor and pads to the next block when the request would straddle the current block, so whenever the edge-key allocation wrapped, `mark` addressed the poisoned tail of the previous block: the install staged a garbage edge key (or the removal looked one up), and the later removal of that rule found its true edge absent — exactly the observed signature (whole key and owner present, `remainingArgsOwners` edge absent, always in `addToHashMemory`'s rule-removal chain). The wrap depends on where the slot's cursor sits inside its block at that moment, which depends on the sequence of LBs the slot processed before — scheduling — so identical proof state aborted intermittently, more often under the CUDA route and RT instrumentation (different phase-3 timing).

**The choice.** `remArgsEdgeKeyInto(argKeyIds, argKeyN, normKeyBlob, normKeyLen, out, outCap)` writes into a caller-owned stack buffer sized by the new `ExpressionAnalyzer::kMaxRemArgsEdgeKeyBytes` (`4 × (2 + MAX_KEY_SLOTS) + kMaxNormKeyBytes`); the four callers (`stageRemainingArgsNormKeyBatch`, `insertRemainingArgsNormKeyBatch`, `removeRuleKeyEntries`, `removeRemainingArgsOwner`) drop their edge-key marks and pops. Bytes staged and looked up are now position-independent; no arena state changes on the edge-key path. The general rule is [I-222](30_invariants.md#i-222).

**Why this and not the offset.** Returning the offset would keep the key on the arena and keep a mark/pop pair at every site; the key is bounded (a few hundred bytes at most) and consumed by one lookup or one stage call, which is Rule 28's stack-array case. It also removes the byte-bump traffic of the edge build from the hottest install loop.

**Rejected.** Poisoning less, or asserting in `alloc` that the returned offset equals the cursor — the wrap is a legitimate arena contract, the bug was the reader's assumption.

**Gate.** `test_memory.cpp` (`rem_args_edge_key_layout` on the new signature; `rem_args_edge_key_independent_of_block_wrap` parks the cursor eight bytes before a block end, checks the key, and pins that the arena places a straddling allocation at the next block); unit tests; shortcut + full pipeline byte-identical to the references.

<a id="d-337"></a>
## D-337 — the gen-scratch registry gets the same reserved single-threaded slot as the string registry, and the `WorkerOwned` early return of the claim handshake is phase-2-only (2026-09-03)


**The choice (maintainer-approved).** Two latent defects found while reading the G-72 section ([G-72](50_gotchas.md#g-72)) are closed. (1) `initGenScratchArenas(logicalCores + 1)`: the request-generation scratch registry carries the worker slots plus one reserved slot, exactly like the string registry (`initScratchArenas(logicalCores + 1)`), so every `g_currentCoreId == -1` fallback (`currentGenSlot`, the open-coded `genScratchArenas.slotCount - 1` sites, and the rule-index staging pool that mirrors the gen slots) resolves to a slot no worker owns. Before, the "reserved" gen slot WAS worker `logicalCores - 1`'s arena and its 32 rule-index stagings — a shared arena between that worker and any non-worker thread that hit the fallback while it ran (a steward IO thread's canonical-reload reverse-index rebuild, a CUDA projection shard, the main thread at a seam that overlaps a worker window). (2) `MemorySteward::claimAndLoadForWork` returned immediately on `WorkerOwned` in EVERY phase; only phase-2 split siblings may share an LB (read-only, I-83). Outside phase 2 the LB is written by its claimant, so the handshake now records the claimant (`Memory::claimHolder`, published right before the release-store of `WorkerOwned`) and asserts that a `WorkerOwned` re-entry comes from that same thread (a seam drain re-claiming what it holds); a foreign holder is two writers on one LB and aborts at the claim instead of corrupting silently.

**Why.** G-72 is a timing-dependent divergence on per-LB state that is deterministic when read single-threaded, so every cross-thread door into per-LB state must be provably closed; these two were open on paper. The instrumented runs of the same day did not observe either door in use (the batch configs run a resident-only steward), so neither is proven to be the G-72 cause — they are removed as candidates, and the claim assert turns the second into a loud failure should it ever occur.

**Rejected.** (a) Waiting on a foreign `WorkerOwned` outside phase 2 instead of asserting — a same-thread re-entry would wait on itself, and a genuine second writer is a bug to see (Rule 19). (b) Keeping the gen registry at `logicalCores` slots and routing the `-1` fallback to the string registry's reserved slot — the two registries have different tiers (page-tier containers versus scratch-fill byte-bump, I-132) and must not share an arena.

**Gate.** `test_steward.cpp` (`claim_and_load_for_work_handshake`: same-thread re-entry in phases 1 and 4, foreign phase-2 sibling; `gen_scratch_registry_has_reserved_slot`), 1624+ unit tests, shortcut + full pipeline byte-identical to the pre-change references with the G-72 traps still armed.

<a id="d-333"></a>
## D-333 — a rule install stages its seven index-map writes per absorb window and every touched map is rewritten once; premises are encoded once per multiplied copy (2026-09-03,, maintainer-directed)


**The choice (maintainer-directed: "static dynamic like temp allocator to convert to cold format at the end").** A rule install (`installExpandedImplication` → `addToHashMemory`, per multiplied copy and per surviving permutation) no longer writes each record into the seven cold index maps (`encodedMap`, `normalizedEncodedKeys`, `normalizedEncodedSubkeys`, `remainingArgsNormalizedEncodedMap`, `remainingArgsOwners`, `originals`, `copyOwners`) as it is produced. It stages the record in the worker slot's staging bound to the instance (`memory_infra/rule_index_staging.hpp`: `RuleStagingRegistry` holds four `RuleIndexStaging` per gen-scratch slot, `acquire`d by the install for its target instance; per map a `RuleIndexStagingSection` — a byte-key interner in first-touch order, per key an arrival-ordered item chain, a page-contiguous payload pool; page tier of the slot's gen-scratch arena, private `DirtyState`, never enrolled in `visitContainers`). The window's closer flushes (`ExpressionAnalyzer::flushRuleIndexStaging`): each touched map is rebuilt ONCE in key-id order, in place and backwards (`HashMap::assignAllRunsGenerated` → `BlobCsrValueStore::rebuildRunsInPlace`: one emit pass buffers the produced runs on scratch, then the tail behind the first produced key is written backwards from the new end — carried-over stretches move once as ranges, produced runs are placed; nothing before the first produced key moves, the memory growth is the delta), every key's run merged exactly as the sequential doors merge — sorted-unique owner runs, arrival-ordered LMV runs, the merged `OwnerSet` record (loose OR, sorted-unique signatures, renumbered sorted-unique pairs), the sorted-unique remaining-args run with one reverse-index edge per genuinely new `NormKey` — and the keys the map lacked are minted after the rebuild in first-touch order. The flush's tables proportional to keys or items ride the page tier; its sorts are block-bounded (`ChunkSortedOrdinals` through `StagedSortedUnique`). The cold bytes after a flush equal the bytes the sequential writes produce, so deload streams, the hashburst dump and every proof artefact are unchanged.

**Windows.** `Memory::ruleStagingArmDepth` is raised around the two mail absorbs of `standardProcessing` (flush before `applyEquiClasses`) and around `applyEquiClasses` (flush at its end, so the compact hook's canonical expansions batch); a removal (`removeRuleFromHashMemory`) and the end-of-apply compaction (`finishRuleRemovals`) flush their instance first and keep the direct doors; an `addToHashMemory` whose exit closes its LB's outermost window (LB seeding, the CE facts, the compressor, an auxiliary rule) closes all four of the LB's instances (`closeRuleIndexStaging` — its nested deposits can run a processing round that stages into any of them; the first slot-resident build flushed only the install's own instance and leaked the others until the slot's pool ran dry at grid creation), and a standalone `makeNormalizedKeysForAdmission` (the twin-oracle use) closes its own staging at exit. A binding changes only at a window close: a mid-window flush (a remover's entry) keeps it, `acquire` takes only unbound stagings (an empty bound one belongs to an open frame that has not staged yet), and a removal acquires nothing. The slot's stagings are asserted unbound at every seam a reader reaches: the phase-2 producer (`performElem2`), the gen-arena releases, `eraseOwnerlessEntries`.

**Premise encode memo (the same commit series, idea C).** Per multiplied copy, `KeyEncodeMemo` (memory.hpp) encodes each premise text once, lazily at the program point that used to encode it first (so the NameMap first-touch mint order is unchanged); the whole-key loop, both subkey loops and the four admission passes read it (the admission installer indexes it through the caller's mask). Each permutation's normalized key is built once incrementally (`appendExprToIntNormalizedKey`), the prefix keys being the slots written so far.

**Two-target build (idea D, the incubator).** A status-3 install (an external-mail absorb) used to run `addToHashMemory` twice with identical inputs — once into `overallHashMemory`, once into the per-burst `workingMemory` — and the second run recomputed every copy, permutation and key (measured at 18-32 % of each incubator batch after the staging landed). `addToHashMemory` now takes an optional `secondTarget`: one build, every staged record written to both stagings (the second target's own admission triggers and admission passes still run against its own maps, after the first target's, per copy). Install-only, never the first target itself (asserted); the direct callers of the local pair are unchanged.

**Why.** The atomic install dissection measured the install at 74 % of the full run's worker-seconds (1,156 of 1,555), of which 36 % was the cold blob pool's tail memmove (every append an in-place CSR splice, 2.79 TB moved per run), 17 % walking and rewriting the remaining-args run whole per copy, 9 % peeking and rebuilding owner runs and subkey records per install, 5 % key mints, and 17 % re-encoding the same premise texts per permutation, prefix and admission pass. Staging turns k writes per key per window into one rebuild per map per window; the memo removes the re-encodes.

**Rejected.** (1) The cold-store hole format (a grown run appended at the pool end, compaction at deload) — a format change under I-98 / I-103 / I-119 that only cuts the cost per write; unnecessary once the flush rebuilds instead of splicing. (2) Per-key splices at the flush — O(pool tail) each. (2b) A whole-map rebuild into scratch columns (the first form of the flush) — it copied every map twice per window (131 worker-s of flush on the full run, 60.7 on IncubatorGauss1 alone) and its map-sized scratch on every worker slot raised the static-pool peak from 23.9k to 37.1k of 49k blocks; the in-place backward rebuild costs one splice's worth at the first produced key and grows memory by the delta only. (2c) A two-pass in-place form (count, then write) — the emitter's merges ran twice (shortcut flush 9.3 worker-s against 5.1); the single emit pass with a produced-run buffer keeps both the one merge and the in-place write. (3) Pre-encoding all premises in index order before the loops — would move a premise's first-touch mint when the first surviving permutation is not the identity (NameMap ids → key bytes → deload stream). (4) Staging on the LB's own arena (the first form) — every window closes inside its task, so the LB never needed to carry the staging, and the pages a window's staging touched stayed pinned to the LB's arena for its life: the static-pool peak rose from 23.9k to 37.1k of 49k blocks in the incubator batches. On the slot's gen-scratch arena the pages return to the slot's free list at the flush and are reused by every LB the slot processes.

**Gate.** Unit tests: `test_key_encode_memo.cpp` (2), `test_rule_index_staging.cpp` (7 differentials: the rebuild primitive against a splice sequence, each section's staged flush against the sequential doors — owner runs, LMV runs, subkey records, remaining-args runs with edge owners and reverse-index answers —, the empty flush, and a flush past one block: 70,000 keys and 140,000 items under one key) and `test_rebuild_in_place.cpp` (3: in-place against the scratch twin over random rounds, `growTo` / `writeRunAt`, the descending shifted move). Pipeline: shortcut runs against  (all 56 theorem + count lines identical, 64 theorems, verifier 9,217 / 0, install 23.5 → 13.3 worker-s of ~125); the full seven-batch run against  (all 139 theorem + count lines identical, `theorems.txt` md5, verifier 141,136 / 0): attributed 1,555 → 909 worker-s, install 1,156 → 322 (+ 131 flush on the whole-map form; the in-place form's numbers in `current_state.md`), IncubatorGauss1 prover 31.4 → 18.6 s, IncubatorGauss2 9.7 → 5.3 s.

<a id="d-332"></a>
## D-332 — in incubator batches the root sentinel's mail log has one reader, the anchor LB: incubator-derived theorem rules reach only the anchor LB, the externals seed is stored in the anchor LB's log (2026-09-02,, maintainer-directed)


**The choice (maintainer-directed).** In an incubator batch (`incubator_mode`), theorem rules derived by the incubator — the in-run proofs compacted by the deferred-compaction drain and the load-time batch of theorems proved by earlier incubator batches — are no longer broadcast to every LB. They reach only the anchor LB `(AnchorIncubatorN[…])`, the root sentinel's one child and the holder of every conjecture goal. The externally provided theorems (the hand-written pool lemmas) keep reaching every LB.

**Why.** The rules have the shape `anchor → head`; the anchor LB fires them and mails the heads down through its own per-step delta, so an LB below the anchor gains nothing from installing the rule itself — it receives the head one cycle later either way. Installing them everywhere was the incubator runtime: `DOOR_INSTALL_IMPLICATION` under the phase-1 mail absorb took 76 % of phase-1 worker time in IncubatorPeano1 (1.34 M installs), 83 % in IncubatorPeano2, 95 % in IncubatorGauss1, 96 % in IncubatorGauss2 (reference ). The externals are different: multi-premise lemmas (fold, sequence, the ES2 / ES3 rules) that fire in the premise LBs below the anchor with those LBs' own premises — without them an ES2 / ES3 LB has nothing but the axioms.

**Mechanism.** Nothing changes on the send side; the change is who reads the root's log. (1) `collectMailAncestors` (the `buildGrid` mail-edge registration) stops the ancestor walk at the anchor LB in incubator mode, so an LB strictly below the anchor never lists the root sentinel as a mail ancestor; the anchor LB keeps its root edge. Everything the root's log carries — the compacts of the deferred-compaction drain, the `updateGlobalDirect` / `updateGlobal` theorem-origin rows, the load-time prior-theorems batch — therefore reaches only the anchor LB, at the unchanged two-cycle (in-run) / burst-1 (load) timing. (2) `broadcastTheorems` takes the storing LB as a parameter: the prior-theorems batch stays in the root's log; in incubator mode the externals batch is stored in the anchor LB's log and self-injected into the anchor LB (`incubatorAnchorLb`, asserting exactly one anchor child), so the anchor LB and every LB below it receive it exactly as before. (3) `isAnchorLb` is the one shared anchor-LB predicate (the D-29 gate, `prehandleAnchor`, the edge pruning). (4) **The anchor LB relays the root's history.** The first full run asserted in the chapter export (`buildStack: no origin found`): a contradiction twin's chapter walks theorem → `expansion` → compact → `compilation`, and the compact's `compilation` row rides only the root's log, which the twin no longer reads. Maintainer-chosen fix: at its status-3 (routing-mail) absorb the anchor LB copies every absorbed origin row into its own `mailOut.exprOriginMap` (`relaysAbsorbedHistory`, the routing-mail origin merge in `standardProcessing`), so its descendants receive one cycle later exactly the rows the root's log used to deliver — history only (Rule 16 / I-44), never the statements; receivers dedup. (5) **Shape routing (maintainer-directed after the second gate).** IncubatorGauss3 (`ban_disintegration: false`) lost `anchor → (EnumerationSet3[2,6,7,10] → interval[1,4,2,7,10])`: its premise LB below the anchor needs a rule from a nested prior-incubator theorem. `anchorOnlyRule` now decides per theorem: anchor-only are the single-premise theorems and the two-premise theorems whose second premise is an operator application and whose head is an equality connecting that operator's bound output to an anchor digit — an anchor slot value, read off the premise so that a loaded theorem of an earlier batch (its first premise is that batch's anchor, bridged in-run by the cross-anchor conjecture `current anchor → previous anchor`) is classified without that anchor being a core expression of the current batch (`anchor → (in2[10,x,3] → (=[x,11]))`, the operator premise is derivable at the anchor); every other nested shape is stored in the anchor LB's log — at load (`broadcastTheorems`'s `nestedStore`, the anchor LB self-injected) and in-run (the compaction drain merges the compact into the anchor LB's `mailOut` as well as the root's, under the anchor's claim). [I-220](30_invariants.md#i-220).

**Rejected.** (0) For the history gap: shipping the carrier's own rows wherever a status-3 `expansion` row is written (every batch's mail content, origin-row order at main-batch receivers may change) and letting `buildStack` look up a compact's `compilation` row at an ancestor (a chapter-export contract change) — both refused for the incubator-confined relay. (a) Injecting the compacts straight into the anchor LB's `mailIn` at the post-join seam — one cycle earlier than today (a timing change), a new inbox writer, and a collision with the rolling-window retirement's every-inbox-empty assert (I-162). (b) A per-batch recipient filter inside `MailLog` — a blob-reference format change in the statified mail pool for a routing decision the edge list already expresses. (c) Narrowing the externals as well — refused by the maintainer: the ES2 / ES3 LBs compute their results from the pool lemmas.

**Known exposure.** Some incubator-derived theorems are nested (`anchor → (A → B)`; 91 of IncubatorPeano1's 1036 theorem lines); their rule needs `A`, local only in premise LBs below the anchor. After the change such a rule fires only where `A` is derivable at the anchor LB. The pipeline gate (per-batch theorem lines against the reference run) is the arbiter.

**Gate.** Unit tests (`test_incubator_mail_routing.cpp`); shortcut run byte-identical (no incubator batch); full seven-batch run against  — theorem lines per batch, `files/theorems/theorems.txt` md5, verifier 0 failures, determinism rerun; RT aggregates in . Results are recorded in `current_state.md` on the branch.
<a id="d-334"></a>
## D-334 — `applyEquiClasses` applies the classes statement-major: one class table per apply, an int-column scan for the affected rows, a per-row rewrite closure staged in a temporary list, one drain per round (2026-09-02,, maintainer-directed)

**What.** The two per-class statement loops of `applyEquiClasses` (Pass 1: delta class × every registry row from its waterline; Pass 2: non-delta class × the rows since its waterline) are replaced by one statement-major batch per fixpoint round, after the hook loops: `buildEquiClassTable` (once per apply — every class with blob view, strong run, rank, due-from position, delta flag; token postings `member id → classes`), `collectEquiAffectedRows` (one pass over the `IntEncodedExpr` int columns; a row is due when a comparable class is due for one of its `argId`s), `stageEquiClosure` (the row and its own staged products as a queue; every comparable class containing an item's argument id runs `enumerateEqClassRewrites`; the former sink's filters in order; products staged in `StagedEquiProducts`, keyed `(scope id ++ text)`), `drainStagedEquiProducts` (the former commit block per product, the `equality1` row under the I-34 gate, one `ordisMerge` pass in `sortStatementRows` order). The negated-equality expander runs once per due row. The hooks, their order and round skips, `enumerateEqClassRewrites`, `updateEquivalenceClasses`, the commit doors and the history shape are unchanged; `applyEquivalenceClass` leaves the tree as the test oracle `applyEquivalenceClassOracle` (D-193 survivorship), and the batch is gated against it on twin LBs. The maintainer's shape: iterate the statements once, apply all classes to a statement in one go, stage the products in a temporary static list that never shifts, convert in one step.

**Why.** The clean shortcut RT table put `AEC_PASS1_APPLY_CLASS` at 27.5 worker-s over 5.74 M (class, statement) calls and `AEC_PASS2_APPLY_CLASS` at 6.3 over 3.22 M: the sweep decoded the statement, sliced its arguments, hashed each for a NameMap lookup, scanned the class members and copied the level run — per pair — to find, almost always, no member argument. The int row already holds the argument ids the rewrite tests membership against.

**Rejected.** (a) One simultaneous token pass per statement (the door's `canonicalFormAtScope` shape, "one product per target scope"): a token can belong to two classes visible at one scope — a descendant class formed before an ancestor class exists, which the D-44 merge never joins — and the registry holds the union of both orbits with chained history rows; a flat multi-class row also fails `check_equality1`'s per-position pair test. The per-row closure keeps the union and the chain. (b) A persistent `token → rows` index maintained at every registry writer: `cleanUpExpressions` compacts the registry after nearly every apply, so it would be rebuilt as often as the per-round scan runs; the scan reads only int columns. Measured first; the index is the follow-on if `AEC_BATCH_SCAN` stays visible. (c) A bulk cold build for the drain: every product write is a tail append on a new key; there is no per-product restructure to batch.

**Consequences.** Hooks run before any statement work of the round (before, class `k`'s hooks preceded class `k`'s loop): the rejected hooks' Site-F parity drop sees products of earlier delta classes one apply later. Statement-major emission changes the NameMap mint order, the first-wins winner among equal products from different rows, and the `ordisMerge` order — hashburst dump and proof-graph bytes differ, verifier check counts may shift deterministically; the gate is the theorem set, verifier 0 failures and a determinism rerun (byte-identity waived by the maintainer). The `startIdx` column grows with delta entries pushed mid-round (hardening; no such push exists). The `cleanUpExpressions` waterline defect found during the design — the compaction never repaired `eqClassSttmntIndexMapMap`, so non-delta classes skipped the rows later registered in the vacated positions — was repaired first, on its own commit (theorem sets identical on both legs, verifier +80 checks in the main block). RT labels: `AEC_BATCH_TABLE`, `AEC_BATCH_SCAN`, `AEC_BATCH_CLOSURE`, `AEC_BATCH_DRAIN`, `AEC_BATCH_ORDIS`; `AEC_PASS1_APPLY_CLASS` and `AEC_PASS2_APPLY_CLASS` are gone, `AEC_PASS2` now wraps the non-delta hook loop only.

**Measured (2026-09-02, vs the waterline-repair commit ).** Shortcut: prover 61.0 → 50.2 s, overall 69.9 → 55.6 s, verifier 9,207 → 9,217 / 0, 64 theorems on both sides with one line differing — the in-run or theorem `or9[1,4,7,9,10]` is constructed with its disjuncts swapped (`or9[1,4,7,10,9]`); its parent implication `(in[9,1]) → (¬preorder[1,4,7,10] → preorder[1,4,7,9])` is level-refused on the reference and registered `direct` on the batch (the goal-discharge verdict is identical on both — refused, levels `0,1,2,4` of five — the batch's row comes through the contradiction-twin discharge; level verdicts are order-dependent, accepted by the maintainer); or-consumed parents never reach `theorems.txt`. Full: `theorems.txt` identical (62), verifier 139,376 → 140,155 / 0, overall 515.5 → 513.3 s, every theorem line of every batch log identical; determinism rerun reproduces every line. RT: `AEC_PASS1_APPLY_CLASS` 27.5 + `AEC_PASS2_APPLY_CLASS` 6.3 worker-s → `AEC_BATCH_CLOSURE` 9.1 + `AEC_BATCH_DRAIN` 1.6 + `AEC_BATCH_SCAN` 0.7 + `AEC_BATCH_ORDIS` 0.6; in the incubator batches the per-round scan is the larger batch row (the persistent token index is the follow-on). Two seams found by the full run and fixed: the compressor-mode `OriginOnly` record beside the row's own seed (one seed + one product per key), and the negated-equality rows re-located by identity because the expander's `addStatement` path can compact the registry mid-loop.

**Contract.** [I-65](30_invariants.md#i-65) (revised).

<a id="d-335"></a>
## D-335 — the processed-or ledger keeps each row's class-canonical id and is re-keyed at the class-change seam; the or-uniqueness probe is an exact id lookup (2026-09-02,, maintainer-directed)

**What.** `Memory::processedOrLedger` rows become packed `(canonical id, original id)` pairs (`packInt32Pair`). `recordProcessedOr` computes the canonical half under the classes present at record time (`canonicalOrIdAtScope` — the door's walk, own-scope bucket, minting the canonical text when it was never interned); `recanonicalizeProcessedOrLedger` recomputes every row of a scope right after `updateEquivalenceClasses` stores a merged class and pushes it to `changedClassesThisStep` — the single place a scope's class bucket changes. `orEquiRepresentativeRecorded` is then one pass over the run comparing ids: canonical half for the equi-variant case, original half for the byte-equal case. The D-331 drain groups by the canonical half instead of canonicalizing each entry itself; the clear paths and the drain's loser retirement keep keying on the original half (the cohort signature, I-167).

**Why.** The clean shortcut RT table (ledger trap compiled out) put `DOOR_OR_EQUI_GATE` at 24 worker-s for 28,931 probes — 0.84 ms each, 11.5 % of attributed time: every or deposit walked the whole per-scope ledger and ran a full `canonicalFormAtScope` on each same-operator record, quadratic in the ors per scope with a class walk as the inner step, paid in full on every miss. The deposit is already door-canonical (I-217), so the walk only compensated for records made stale by later merges; re-keying the records where the merge happens costs one canonicalization per row per class change instead of per row per deposit. Maintainer ruling: "ledger can be held in canonical form and updated on equi class change".

**Rejected.** (a) Lazy re-key with a per-scope class generation stamp — fewer re-keys on scopes that see no later deposit, but a second piece of state to keep in step; the eager seam is one call in one place. (b) Folding the ledger into the statement registry by re-keying registry rows instead of dropping them in `SP_CLEANUP_EXPRESSIONS` — removes the structure altogether, but changes I-85 / I-217 semantics and is a design of its own. (c) Keeping only the canonical id — the original id is what every clear path and the D-331 drain key on.

**Consequences.** Probe cost is the run length. Any NEW writer of `equivalenceClassesMap` must call the seam or the rows go stale (I-219's fix line). Semantics are unchanged — the former probe matched canonical(record) == deposit or byte-equality, and the two halves reproduce exactly those two matches. Gate (shortcut, CUDA phase 2, ledger trap compiled out on both sides): verifier 9,207 / 0, theorem list byte-identical, unit tests 1,580 / 1,580; prover 77.8 s -> 58.2 s, phase-3 wall 58.2 s -> 39.9 s, `DOOR_OR_EQUI_GATE` 24.16 -> 0.13 worker-s (phase 3) and 2.25 -> 0.02 (phase 1) at unchanged hit counts (28,931 / 5,905); the seam's cost shows as `ADDSTMT_UPDATE_EQUI_CLASSES` 4.28 -> 4.85 worker-s.
